newsitem.title: UK: Accounting system for UK National Savings queried.
newsitem.headline: Accounting system for UK National Savings queried.

text.p: British watchdog body the National Audit Office (NAO) said on Friday it had identified problems in the accounting system at the state-owned National Savings agency, which weaken controls against fraud and error.

It said "significant unexplained balances" exist on two suspense accounts, while various methods used to assess the agency's liability to investors show differences amounting to millions of pounds sterling.

"Although the level of detected fraud at the Agency is low, the problems identified weaken the Agency's financial control systems whose purposes include the prevention and detection of error and fraud," the NAO said in a report.

"They also make it difficult to establish the precise liability of the Exchequer to National Savings' investors, with the possibility that provision may have to be made in the future from public funds to meet liabilities to investors not currently reflected in the accounts."
The agency exists to help fund Britain's National Debt by offering a range of personal savings products to the public.

The NAO said in the last audited accounts for December 31, 1994, 37 million stg was shown as being owed by investors to the Unallocated Monies suspense account. "However, investors cannot owe money to the agency since their accounts are not credited until money has been received," the report said.
The NAO said there were unsubstantiated amounts shown in another suspense account totalling 14.1 million stg.
"Without regular and full reconciliation of balances on all suspense accounts, the Agency's systems of internal control, including those to prevent and detect fraud, are weakened," it said.
"The National Audit Office recommend that the Agency give priority to investigating fully the balances on these suspense accounts."
In addition, the NAO said there were discrepancies in the figures for the agency's total liability to investors as between the various methods it used to calculate them.

One method was to add deposits and interest earned to the previous year's figure and deduct amounts repaid. There were also two methods under which balances in the customer accounting systems were totalled.

In the end-1994 accounts, there was a difference in the figures obtained by the first method and one of the others of 2.1 million stg in respect of investment deposits and 711,000 stg in respect of ordinary deposits.
